text.what: A tie, either made in cloth and thread or copied in stone and metal. Two kinds sit under one heading: the knot that is actually tied — a red string on a wrist, a thousand stitches in a soldier's belt, rushes woven on a feast day — and the knot that is depicted, cut in jasper or drawn as a hieroglyph, with nothing to untie.
text.story:
Egypt gives the depicted knot its clearest case. The tyet resembles a knot of cloth and may have started as a bandage to absorb menstrual blood. An early example comes from a First Dynasty tomb at Helwan, excavated by Zaki Saad in the 1940s — old enough to predate the first written references to Isis, whom it was later tied to. From the early New Kingdom, roughly 1550 BCE, tyet amulets went into the wrappings, usually on the upper torso, and from then to the end of dynastic Egypt few people were buried without one. Chapter 156 of the Book of the Dead calls for a tyet of red jasper at the mummy's neck and says the power of Isis will protect the body and drive away whoever would commit a crime against it. Green faience examples were made too, the colour standing for renewed life. The tyet can be compared with the Minoan sacral knot at Knossos — a knot with a projecting loop — and the comparison is offered as a resemblance, not a descent.

The tied knot is a different object with a different working part: somebody's hands did it, at a named time, and it can be undone. Bulgarian and Macedonian martenitsi are twisted red and white yarn, given never bought, worn from 1 March and taken off at the sight of a stork or a blossoming tree — sometimes tied then onto a fruit tree. Romanian mărțișor uses the same two threads and is described by observers as funia anului, the year's rope, winding summer into winter. Irish Brigid's crosses are woven from straw or rushes on 1 February and hung in the rafters. Japanese senninbari carry a thousand knots, each made by a different woman, for a soldier going to war.

Undoing is part of the grammar. Islamic hadith describe a charm worked against Muhammad; in one variant he is cured only after the charm — a knot — is taken and taken apart. *Inference —* a knot is the one amulet form that carries its own cancellation in its shape, which is why so many traditions put a date on when it comes off.
